title: An Ocean-World Candidate
sub: A sub-Neptune that just might hold water
blurb: K2-18 is a dim red dwarf 124 light-years away, circled by K2-18 b — a world larger than Earth, sitting squarely in the habitable zone. After a string of headline discoveries it has become the most closely studied candidate for a planet that could carry an ocean.

title: A Cool Red Dwarf
sub: Smaller and dimmer than the Sun
blurb: K2-18 is an M-type red dwarf — only about 40% the Sun's width and roughly half as hot. Such small, frugal stars burn so slowly they can shine for trillions of years, far longer than the Sun ever will.

title: Between Two Worlds
sub: Bigger than Earth, smaller than Neptune
blurb: K2-18 b is a sub-Neptune: about 2.6 times Earth's width and eight times its mass. Worlds in this in-between size — too big to be rocky, too small to be a gas giant — are the most common kind we have found, yet we have nothing like them at home.

title: In the Habitable Zone
blurb: Because its star is so dim, K2-18 b can huddle close — orbiting every 33 days — and still receive about as much warmth as Earth. That places it in the habitable zone, the band where a world could hold liquid water on its surface.

title: Caught in Transit
sub: Found as it crossed its star
blurb: K2-18 b was discovered in 2015 by NASA's repurposed Kepler telescope, on its K2 mission. Each time the planet passes in front of its star it blocks a tiny fraction of the light — a faint, repeating dip that betrays an unseen world.

title: Reading the Starlight
blurb: When the planet transits, a little starlight filters through its atmosphere on the way to us. Each gas absorbs its own set of colours, stamping dark lines into the spectrum — so by splitting that light apart, we can read which molecules float in an alien sky.

title: Water in the Air
sub: A first for a habitable-zone world
blurb: In 2019 astronomers found the unmistakable fingerprint of water vapour in K2-18 b's atmosphere — the first time water had ever been detected around a planet in the habitable zone. It turned a faint dot into one of the most exciting worlds known.

title: A Hycean World?
sub: An ocean beneath a hydrogen sky
blurb: In 2023 the JWST detected methane and carbon dioxide — but little ammonia — in K2-18 b's air, exactly what you might expect above a vast ocean cloaked in hydrogen. This "Hycean" picture is tantalising, but a tentative hint of life-linked gas remains hotly debated.

title: 124 Light-Years Away
blurb: K2-18 lies about 124 light-years away in the constellation Leo. The light we study from it tonight set out in the 1900s — so every measurement we make is a glimpse of the system as it was more than a century ago.
